'''William Ian Gasarch''' ({{IPAc-en|ɡ|ə|ˈ|s|ɑː|r|ʃ}} {{Respell|gə|SARSH}};<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TXJ6fYF9em8|title=Rectangle Free Colorings – William Gasarch|work=YouTube|date=May 8, 2017|accessdate=12 October 2022}}</ref> born 1959<ref>{{cite web |title=Still Typecasting from Dagstuhl |url=https://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/2018/09/still-typecasting-from-dagstuhl.html |website=Computational Complexity Weblog |publisher=Lance Fortnow and William Gasarch |accessdate=27 September 2018}}</ref>) is an American computer scientist known for his work in [[computational complexity theory]], [[computability theory]], [[computational learning theory]], and [[Ramsey theory]]. He is currently a professor at the [[University of Maryland]] Department of Computer Science with an affiliate appointment in Mathematics.

Gasarch is a frequent mentor of high school student research projects; one of these, with [[Jacob Lurie]], won the 1996 [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] for Lurie.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199607/comm-conway.pdf|title=Budding Mathematician Wins Westinghouse Competition|last1=Conway|first1=John H.|last2=Jackson|first2=Allyn|date=July 1996|publisher=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|access-date=2016-09-26}}</ref> He has co-blogged on computational complexity with [[Lance Fortnow]] since 2007.  He was book review editor for [[ACM SIGACT]] NEWS from 1997 to 2015.

==Education==
Gasarch received his doctorate in computer science from [[Harvard University|Harvard]] in 1985, advised by [[Harry R. Lewis]].  His thesis was titled ''Recursion-Theoretic Techniques in Complexity Theory and Combinatorics''.<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=39665}}</ref> He was hired into a tenure track professorial job at the University of Maryland in the Fall of 1985. He was promoted to associate professor with tenure in 1991, and to full professor in 1998.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/billcv.pdf|title=Curriculum vitae|first=William|last=Gasarch|publisher=U. Maryland Computer Science|date=March 16, 2023|access-date=2024-02-14}}</ref>

==Work==
Gasarch co-founded (with Richard Beigel) the field of  Bounded Queries in Recursion Theory<ref>http://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/papers/gems.pdf Gems in the Field of Bounded Queries by William Gasarch, 2003</ref> and has written many papers in the area capped off by a book on the topic  co-authored with Georgia Martin,  titled ''Bounded Queries in Recursion Theory''.<ref>https://www.springer.com/us/book/9780817639662 Bounded Queries in Recursion Theory (with Georgia Martin), Birkhauser, 1999</ref> He has published books such as ''Problems with a Point'',<ref>https://www.worldscientific.com/worldscibooks/10.1142/11261 Problems with a Point Exploring Math and Computer Science, 2019</ref> a book with a broad view on mathematics and theoretical computer science which he co-authored with [[Clyde Kruskal]] and includes works by other professors such as [[David Eppstein]].<ref>https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789813279735_0014 Chapter 14: Is This Problem Too Hard for a High School Math Competition?, 2019</ref> He also co-founded the subfield of recursion-theoretic  inductive inference named ''Learning via Queries''<ref>http://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/papers/lvqsur.pdf A Survey of Inductive Inference with an Emphasis on Queries, Gasarch and Smith, 1997</ref> with [[Carl Herbert Smith|Carl Smith]]. More recently he has been more involved with combinatorics, notably Ramsey Theory.<ref>{{Cite journal |arxiv = 1005.3749|last1 = Gasarch|first1 = William|title = Lower Bounds on the van der Waerden Numbers: Randomized- and Deterministic-Constructive|journal = Electronic Journal of Combinatorics |volume = 18|issue = 64|last2 = Haeupler|first2 = Bernhard|year = 2011| article-number=P64 |doi = ==Blog==
Lance Fortnow began writing a blog on theoretical computer science with an emphasis on complexity theory in 2002.<ref>http://blog.computationalcomplexity.org/ Computational Complexity Weblog</ref> Gasarch was a frequent guest blogger until 2007 when he became an official co-blogger.
